sections.title: Purpose of the Corporation
sections.content:
The RFC reproduces the articles of incorporation of the Internet Society, published at the request of the poisson working group. The articles establish a non-profit corporation without capital stock, organized for educational, charitable, and scientific purposes.

Those purposes include supporting the Internet's technical evolution, educating the public about Internet technology, promoting educational uses, and providing a forum to explore applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The articles describe an organization set up for educational, charitable, and scientific purposes. They include supporting the Internet's technical development and teaching people about it.

sections.title: Membership and the Board of Trustees
sections.content:
The articles provide for classes of members, with membership qualifications and rights, including voting rights, set out in the bylaws. The corporation's board is called the Board of Trustees.

The initial Board of Trustees has fourteen members named in the articles. The bylaws determine how later trustees are elected or appointed.
sections.plainLanguage: The bylaws set member rights and explain how trustees are chosen. The articles name the initial Board of Trustees.

sections.title: Amendments and Dissolution
sections.content:
Most amendments to the articles require an affirmative vote of at least four-fifths of trustees then in office. Changing Article 7 requires unanimous consent of those trustees.

If the corporation dissolves, its remaining assets, after liabilities are addressed, go to qualifying educational, charitable, or scientific organizations as determined under the articles.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing most articles requires a large majority of trustees, while changing Article 7 requires every trustee's consent. If the corporation closes, remaining assets go to qualifying organizations.
